fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think about this a lot, partly because it rhymes with things I've seen in architecture research. If you look at the history of vision, we kept adding hand-designed structure: anchor boxes, feature pyramids, carefully tuned augmentation pipelines. Then the models got bigger and better trained, and a lot of that structure got absorbed. ConvNeXt was partly a lesson in that direction, that a lot of what we attributed to clever architecture was really about the training recipe and scale.

Agent scaffolding feels like the same story, maybe a few years behind. Right now the scaffold is doing real work. It decomposes the task, it manages memory, it decides when to call a tool, it retries when something fails. Those are all things the base model is not yet reliable enough to do on its own over a long horizon. So the scaffold is compensating for weaknesses in the model, and it's valuable.

But I think most of that compensation is temporary. As models get trained more directly on long-horizon tasks, on tool use, on recovering from their own mistakes, the scaffold stops being a source of capability and starts being a constraint. You see this already. A rigid planning loop that helped a weaker model can actually hurt a stronger one, because you're forcing it to think in a way it would not have chosen.

What I don't think goes away is the part of the scaffold that encodes things the model genuinely cannot know. Permissions, what actions are allowed, which resources are available, how to verify outcomes against the real world. That's not capability, that's interface and control, and I'd expect it to get thinner but more principled over time.

So if I were building scaffolding today, I would try to be honest about which pieces are crutches and which pieces are infrastructure. The crutches you should expect to delete. The infrastructure you should design carefully, because that's what survives.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because there's a pattern we've seen many times in deep learning. Whenever the base models are weak, people build a lot of structure around them: hand-designed pipelines, special modules, careful prompting, multi-stage workflows. Then the models get stronger and much of that structure becomes unnecessary, or even starts to hurt. It's basically the bitter lesson playing out again.

With agents, a lot of today's scaffolding exists to compensate for things the model can't yet do reliably. It can't plan over long horizons, so we break tasks into subtasks for it. It loses track of state, so we build memory systems and summarization loops. It makes mistakes it doesn't notice, so we add verifier steps, retries, and reflection prompts. These help a lot right now. But many of them encode our guesses about how the problem should be decomposed. As models improve, they often find a better decomposition on their own, and our rigid structure gets in the way.

So I expect a large share of the clever, task-specific scaffolding to get thinner over time. I don't think scaffolding goes away entirely, though. I'd separate it into two kinds.

The first kind compensates for model weakness. That's the kind that will mostly disappear, the way hand-engineered features disappeared once we had good end-to-end learning.

The second kind is really the interface between the model and the world: what tools it can access, how it sees a file system or a browser, how permissions and sandboxing work, how it gets feedback from the environment. That's less about making up for a weak model and more about defining the action space and the environment. If anything, that layer becomes more important as models get more capable, because a capable model with a bad interface is still bottlenecked. And when agents act in the real world, you want guardrails, logging, and human checkpoints, no matter how smart the model is.

There's also a training angle. A lot of what's scaffolding today becomes training data or training signal tomorrow. If you have a workflow that reliably produces good trajectories, you can train on those, and the behavior moves into the weights. So the scaffolding acts as a bootstrap: you use it to get the model to a point where it doesn't need it anymore.

My practical advice, for researchers or people building products, is to hold scaffolding loosely. Use it, because it gets you results now. But design things so the model can take over more of the decision-making as it improves, and don't invest so heavily in an elaborate pipeline that it becomes a liability when the next model generation comes out. The things that tend to last are good environments, good tools, and good ways of evaluating whether the agent actually did the job, more than the specific orchestration logic in the middle.

r002.rationale: It predicts that as models improve, much task-specific scaffolding will become unnecessary and recommends designing systems so models can take over more decisions.

r003.rationale: It explicitly advises letting the model take over more of the decision-making as it improves.

fable-5.text:
I think the honest answer is that most scaffolding is a temporary patch, and we've seen this movie before in computer vision. When I started working on object detection, the pipelines were full of hand-designed components — region proposals, anchor boxes, non-maximum suppression, carefully tuned post-processing stages. Each piece existed because the model itself wasn't capable enough to handle that part of the problem. And one by one, as models got better, those components got absorbed into the model and the pipelines became simpler, not more complex. End-to-end learning kept winning.

I expect the same dynamic with agents. A lot of what we call scaffolding today — elaborate prompt chains, hand-crafted subtask decompositions, retry logic, routing between specialized models — is really us compensating for the model's weaknesses in planning and long-horizon coherence. Every time the base model takes a step up in capability, some fraction of that scaffolding becomes dead weight, and sometimes it actively hurts, because you've baked in assumptions about how the model should break down a problem when the model now has a better idea itself.

That said, I don't think scaffolding goes to zero, and it's useful to distinguish two kinds. There's scaffolding that compensates for model deficiencies, which I'd bet against long-term. And there's scaffolding that defines the interface to the world — tool access, sandboxing, permissions, how the agent reads and writes persistent state. That second category isn't about intelligence at all; it's about what the agent is allowed to touch and how we verify what it did. That layer probably gets thinner and more standardized, but it stays, the same way operating systems stayed even as applications got smarter.

So if I were advising a student or a startup, I'd say: be suspicious of any system whose value comes from cleverness in the orchestration layer, because that's exactly the part the next model release erodes. The durable work is in the environment, the evaluation, and the data — the things that remain valuable no matter how capable the model underneath becomes.

r002.rationale: It predicts that as base models improve, some scaffolding becomes unnecessary or harmful, reducing what is needed for a given level of capability.

r003.rationale: It suggests that models may develop better plans than hand-crafted orchestration, but does not clearly recommend letting models make more system decisions themselves.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, my instinct comes from having watched this play out in vision. Object detection in 2015 was a pipeline: region proposals, anchor boxes, hand-tuned post-processing, multiple stages stitched together with heuristics. Every one of those pieces existed because the model couldn't do that part itself. And one by one they got absorbed — into the architecture, into the loss, into the data. The scaffolding was real engineering, it was necessary, and it was temporary.

I think a lot of agent scaffolding is in that category. Chain-of-thought is the cleanest example in our own recent memory: it started as a prompting trick, something you bolted on from outside, and now it just lives in the weights. Nobody writes "think step by step" anymore. So when I see an elaborate multi-agent orchestration with a planner and a critic and a verifier, my prior is that a good fraction of that structure is a description of the current model's failure modes, and it will get eaten.

But I'd separate two things that both get called scaffolding. One is compensating for something the model can't do yet — plan over long horizons, notice it's stuck, decompose a task. That shrinks as models improve. The other is connecting the model to the world: tool access, permissions, state that outlives the context window, sandboxing, the ability to actually observe consequences. That isn't scaffolding, that's infrastructure, and I think it gets *more* important as models get stronger, because a more capable agent is one you're willing to give more reach.

The part that worries me methodologically is evaluation. When you report that your scaffold gives a twenty-point improvement, that number is entangled with the specific model you tuned it against. The useful diagnostic — and this is basically the same thing we argued about pruning, that you have to compare against a properly trained simple baseline — is to ask whether the scaffold still helps on the strongest model you have access to. If the gain evaporates as the base model improves, you've measured a deficiency, not discovered a method. If it survives, you've probably found something structural.

So I don't think the work is wasted. Scaffolding is how we locate the boundary of what models can't do, and increasingly it's how we generate the data that pushes the boundary. You just shouldn't be surprised, or offended, when your scaffold gets amortized into the next checkpoint.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think of scaffolding as something that compensates for what the model can't do yet, so it tends to shrink as models improve. A lot of early agent work, like hand-designed planning loops, elaborate prompt chains, and rigid routing between sub-agents, was really a workaround for models that couldn't plan, keep track of state, or recover from their own mistakes. Once the model can do those things natively, the workaround becomes dead weight, and sometimes it hurts, because it constrains the model to a workflow a stronger model would have gone beyond. This is the bitter lesson again. Hand-engineered structure helps in the short term, and then general capability and scale absorb it.

But I don't think scaffolding disappears. It changes from "make the model smarter" to "connect the model to the world." Even a very capable model needs tools, a way to act in an environment, access to the right context, memory over long horizons, and some mechanism for checking its work. That part is more like infrastructure or interface design than reasoning scaffolding, and I think it stays important. A brilliant person with no computer, no files, and no way to run anything is still limited.

So when I see a new scaffolding trick, I ask whether it's adding information or capability the model fundamentally lacks, or just patching a weakness that the next model generation will probably fix. The first kind lasts, and the second kind is likely to be obsolete in a year. The practical consequence is to keep scaffolding simple and modular, so you can strip pieces out as the model improves. If your system is so tightly coupled to one model's quirks that you can't remove anything, you'll fall behind quickly.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think scaffolding will shrink, but it won't disappear. A lot of what we built around models a couple of years ago, like elaborate prompt chains and hand-written planners that spelled out every step, was compensating for weak capability. As models get better at following long instructions and planning on their own, that rigid structure starts to hurt more than it helps.

But I'd separate two kinds of scaffolding. Pieces that encode the model's weaknesses, like "retry if the test fails" or "check your output before committing," will likely get absorbed into training. Pieces that encode facts about the environment, like which tools exist, what permissions you have, how state persists across sessions, and what counts as done, don't go away just because the model is smarter. A brilliant engineer still needs a repo, a CI system, and a ticket tracker.

So I think the scaffold shifts from a crutch to an interface. The interesting question is less "how do we guide the model step by step" and more "what should the model be responsible for, and what should the system guarantee?" I'd even guess we end up with more scaffolding in some respects, not less, once agents run for hours or days in complicated environments. What I'm least sure about is where that boundary settles.

astra-6.text:
I think the role of scaffolding will change as the models get better. Today, you might need to break a task into very specific steps, tell the model when to check its work, and build a lot of logic around how it recovers from mistakes. I would expect stronger models to handle more of those decisions themselves, so some of that scaffolding can become simpler.

That makes me a little cautious about investing too heavily in a complicated pipeline that compensates for the weaknesses of one particular model. When the next model comes along, you should test whether those extra steps still help. They may actually constrain what the model can do.

But the model still needs access to tools, useful context, and feedback from the environment. Those interfaces remain important. So I’d try to build a relatively simple system, measure where it fails, and add structure where there’s a clear benefit. Then keep revisiting those choices as the underlying model improves.

sol-6.1.text:
My intuition is that the scaffolding will become simpler as the models become more capable. A lot of what we put around a model today is compensating for its weaknesses. We explicitly tell it how to break down a task, when to reflect, when to call a tool. If the model can learn to do those things reliably, you may not need to specify that whole process externally.

That makes it a little tricky to decide what to invest in. You can spend a lot of effort building a complicated workflow, and then the next model can do the same thing with a much simpler setup. So I would be interested in how much of the improvement comes from the scaffolding, and whether that improvement persists when you use a stronger underlying model.

But I don’t think everything around the model disappears. It still needs access to tools, to the environment, to information that isn’t in its parameters. There’s still a system to build. I think the boundary shifts: the model takes on more of the decisions that we currently encode by hand, and the surrounding system focuses more on giving it the right access and feedback.

terra-5.6.text:
I think scaffolding becomes more important, not less. As models get stronger, the bottleneck shifts from whether they can solve an individual subproblem to how we decompose a long-horizon task, provide the right context, verify intermediate results, and recover from mistakes. A capable model can be a great worker, but without a good scaffold it may still spend effort in the wrong place or lose track of the overall objective.

At the same time, we should be careful not to mistake scaffolding for intelligence. A lot of current agent systems work through fairly brittle prompt engineering, tool loops, and hand-designed workflows. Better models will absorb some of that complexity. But for real-world tasks—where you need memory, planning, interaction with tools, and reliable feedback—the system around the model will remain a major part of the capability.

But it won’t disappear, because real-world agents still need interfaces, memory, permissions, feedback, and reliability guarantees. The key question is which capabilities should be learned by the model and which should be enforced by the surrounding system.

luna-5.6.text: I think the role of scaffolding will evolve rather than disappear. Today, a lot of scaffolding compensates for weaknesses in the model—breaking a task into steps, prompting it repeatedly, or asking it to critique its own answer. As the underlying models become more capable, those basic techniques may become less necessary. But we’ll still need scaffolding to give the model access to tools, memory, feedback, and ways of verifying its work. The bottleneck shifts from getting the model to produce a plausible answer to building a reliable system that can pursue a long-horizon objective, recover from mistakes, and know when it is uncertain. So the best agents may have simpler prompts, but more carefully designed interfaces and feedback loops around the model.
